ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The research presented in this manuscript has been approved by the local ethics committee at the Leibniz-Institut für Wissensmedien (Knowledge Media Research Center) (LEK 2025/22).
Participants were assigned to either the high-variation or the low-variation expertise condition and a sequential chain position before performing sequential collaboration for six different topics.
One participant was excluded due to technical issues during participation; another 19 participants were excluded due to duplicates in chain position.

In the high-variation condition, the six pieces of information presented to participants were filled such that each of the remaining ten pieces of information for each topic was mentioned thrice throughout the sequential chain.
Participants were recruited for a 20-minute collaborative wiki-style study and provided their informed consent.
In each trial, participants were presented with eight pieces of information and were given 60 seconds to read them thoroughly.
Afterward, participants were automatically directed to the editing page where the text of a previous participant was displayed in an open text box ready for editing.
Participants were required to stay for at least 30 seconds on the page before they could continue and could edit the text for a maximum of 5 minutes.
After completing sequential collaboration for all six topics, participants provided demographic information, were debriefed and thanked for their participation.
All participants provided written consent before participating in the presented experiment.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

table.title: Sequential collaboration: info sharing, expertise variation I
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
Hypothesis 1: High variation in contributors' expertise leads to more pieces of information included into the common product than low variation in expertise. 
Hypothesis 2: High variation in contributors' expertise leads to implementation of new information into the common product earlier in the sequential chain than low variation in expertise. 
Hypothesis 3: High variation in contributors' expertise leads to more deletions of content than low variation in expertise.
table.design_dependent_variables:
Pieces of information mentioned in the common product (Hypothesis 1, Hypothesis 2).
Pieces of information deleted in a sequential step (Hypothesis 3).
table.study_design_overview:
Participants will perform sequential collaboration in sequential chains of six, including the starting text and five participants consecutively adjusting it. Participants perform sequential collaboration for six topics. For each topic, they receive 8 out of a total of 13 pieces of information, 2 of them included in the starting text. Based on this information, participants collaboratively write a Wikipedia style text.
Between-subjects condition: High variation in expertise vs. low variation in expertise
- High variation condition: Each piece of information is presented exactly thrice to three different participants in the sequential chain.
- Low variation condition: Five pieces of information are presented to all participants in the sequential chain, the remaining five pieces of information are only presented to one participant.
table.statistical_tests: We conduct hierarchical linear regressions to test our hypothesis with pieces of information mentioned (Hypothesis 1 & 2) or deleted (Hypothesis 3) as dependent variable and chain position and condition (high vs. low expertise variability) as independent variables. We will take into account the nested structure of our data with random intercepts for participants and items and consider random slopes if the model still converges.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Participants are excluded from the study during participation if they switch to other programs or browser windows more than five times during the study against repeated warnings.
Participants are excluded from data analysis if they engage in behavior that suggests low effort or interest or looking up external information in three or more topics presented. This is indicated by deleting the total entry created by previous participants, adding information that is unrelated to the topic, or adding information that has not been presented to them. Participants following in the sequential chain are excluded as well.
table.sample_size: We will recruit at least 400 student participants for this experiment.
table.additional_comments: We will exploratorily investigate the quality of written texts as well as the amount of text adjusted / maintained in each sequential step.

Participants were recruited for a 20-minute collaborative wiki-style study and provided their informed consent.
In each trial, participants were presented with eight pieces of information and were given 60 seconds to read them thoroughly.
Afterward, participants were automatically directed to the editing page where the text of a previous participant was displayed in an open text box ready for editing.
Participants were required to stay for at least 30 seconds on the page before they could continue and could edit the text for a maximum of 5 minutes.
After completing sequential collaboration for all six topics, participants provided demographic information, were debriefed and thanked for their participation.
All participants provided written consent before participating in the presented experiment.

info.title: Expertise Diversity Enhances Information Sharing in Wiki settings: Evidence from Sequential Collaboration
keywords: Writing -Original Draft Preparation; Joachim Kimmerle: Conceptualization

text.text: Online collaborative projects like Wikipedia rely on sequential collaboration, where individual contributors iteratively revise a shared product.

While previous research has examined wikis for collaborative writing and sequential collaboration for numerical judgments, little is known about the cognitive mechanisms underlying information sharing in such settings.
The present study bridges research on collaborative writing, group information sharing, and cognitive models of sequential collaboration.
Drawing on a computational model of sequential collaboration, we tested whether higher variation in contributors' expertise facilitates the integration of information into a shared text.
In an experiment with 413 participants, we demonstrate that information accumulation increased throughout the sequential chain but at a decreasing rate.
Consistent with model predictions, higher expertise variation resulted in more information being incorporated into the shared text.
Contrary to expectations, expertise variation did not affect the speed of information accumulation, nor did it increase information deletions.
These findings demonstrate that predictions derived from a cognitive model of numerical judgment formation generalize to information-sharing contexts.
More broadly, the results suggest that diversity in contributors' knowledge can improve collaborative knowledge construction in sequential environments.
This research adds to evidence that sequential collaboration is an effective mechanism for integrating distributed knowledge in online collaborative systems.
Online collaborative projects rapidly emerged about 25 years ago.
These projects fundamentally reshaped how individuals collaborate allowing collaboration across place and time.

Prominent examples are Wikipedia and OpenStreetMap which are highly successful considering their accuracy and extent (El-Ashmawy, 2016; García del Valle et al., 2018; Giles, 2005; Mesgari et al., 2015; H. Zhang & Malczewski, 2017) and have been extensively researched in the past (Okoli et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2026).

text.text: In sequential collaboration, one contributor starts a sequential chain by creating an entry.
This entry is then sequentially adjusted or maintained by subsequent contributors encountering it.

Projects and interventions relying on a wiki structure have been extensively researched in the context of computer-supported collaborative learning (Jeong et al., 2019; Kimmerle et al., 2015; Zheng et al., 2015).

text.text: Here, wikis are examined as a potential learning intervention for students.
Even though not explicitly labeled as such, the examined projects and interventions typically relied on sequential collaboration.
Research on computer-supported collaborative learning typically focuses on individual learning and the generation of a common product.
Individual cognitive processes determining which information contributors enter into a collaboratively written text under what conditions is typically not examined.
The most central component of online collaborative projects is information sharing.

In a meta-analysis, Mesmer-Magnus and DeChurch (2009) demonstrated that information sharing is improved when tasks are highly demonstrable, discussions are structured, and group members are more cooperative, which overall leads to better group decisions.
text.formatted: In a meta-analysis, <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Mesmer-Magnus and DeChurch (2009)</ref> demonstrated that information sharing is improved when tasks are highly demonstrable, discussions are structured, and group members are more cooperative, which overall leads to better group decisions.

text.text: A specific paradigm investigating group information sharing and subsequent decision making is the hidden profile paradigm (Lu et al., 2012; Stasser & Titus, 1985).
text.formatted: A specific paradigm investigating group information sharing and subsequent decision making is the hidden profile paradigm <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Lu et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Stasser & Titus, 1985)</ref>.

text.text: Research examining hidden profiles consistently showed that individuals consider unshared information only available to one group member too little and shared information available to all group members too much resulting in inaccurate group decisions (Lu et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Research examining hidden profiles consistently showed that individuals consider unshared information only available to one group member too little and shared information available to all group members too much resulting in inaccurate group decisions <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Lu et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, Mesmer-Magnus and DeChurch (2009) recommend highly demonstrable tasks, structured information sharing, and a cooperative climate to foster information sharing and subsequent decisions.

This can potentially be achieved through sequential collaboration as it provides structured collaboration in which contributors can remain anonymous reducing unwanted biases and directing contributors attention and focus to the common product of their collaboration.

Recently, work on sequential collaboration emerged outside computer-supported collaborative learning, namely for rank order problems (Miller & Steyvers, 2011) and for numerical judgment formation (e.g., Mayer & Heck, 2024).
text.formatted: Recently, work on sequential collaboration emerged outside computer-supported collaborative learning, namely for rank order problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Miller & Steyvers, 2011)</ref> and for numerical judgment formation (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Mayer & Heck, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These accounts use minimal sequential collaboration tasks in which contributors are only confronted with the most recent state of the common group product and receive no information about the (number of) previous contributors, no change history, and do not have access to discussion forums or comments.

This research has more strongly focused on the accuracy of the collaborative estimate (i.e., rank order or numerical judgment, Mayer & Heck, 2024; Miller & Steyvers, 2011), features of current contributors (Mayer et al., 2023), information about previous contributors (Mayer & Kimmerle, 2025) and information about the sequential chain (Fischer et al., 2026) as influences on the contribution process and investigated variations of the collaboration process (Mayer et al., 2025).

text.text: Based on this work, a cognitive model formalizing the findings and theoretical assumptions was developed (Mayer, 2026; Mayer & Heck, 2025).

text.text: Other potentially more successful forms of information sharing were neglected even though they are more prevalent in online settings and often yield a shared product.

Finally, cognitive sequential-collaboration research has focused on numerical judgment formation and explored individual conditions of successful collaboration, but did not apply their results to more realistic sequential-collaboration settings.

This work seeks to take a first step in combining these strands of research and systematically examine sequential collaboration building on a cognitive model of sequential collaboration for numerical judgment formation but using more realistic scenarios of information sharing as found in online collaborative projects.

Thereby, we focus on individual contributors and investigate cognitive mechanisms of sequential collaboration for information sharing, which in turn can help gain deeper insights into optimal conditions for collaboration on a shared product.

From the perspective of computer-supported collaborative learning, collaborative writing tools have been examined in various educational contexts (Mindel & Verma, 2006; Wheeler et al., 2008; Zheng et al., 2015).
text.formatted: From the perspective of computer-supported collaborative learning, collaborative writing tools have been examined in various educational contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Mindel & Verma, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Wheeler et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Zheng et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Wikis allow learners to engage in a joint task, to communicate, share resources, engage in productive collaborative learning processes, engage in co-construction, monitor and regulate collaborative learning and find and build groups and communities (Jeong & Hmelo-Silver, 2016), which result in a medium-sized learning effect (Jeong et al., 2019).

text.text: However, students typically need support for adequate learning (Zheng et al., 2015) and as also observed in online collaborative projects (Arazy & Nov, 2010; Ortega et al., 2008) there is severe inequality in the extent to which learners contribute (Judd et al., 2010).

text.text: From a theoretical perspective, computer-supported collaborative learning was often considered as a co-evolution process (Cress et al., 2016; Cress & Kimmerle, 2008; Kimmerle et al., 2015).
text.formatted: From a theoretical perspective, computer-supported collaborative learning was often considered as a co-evolution process <ref type="bibr">(Cress et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Cress & Kimmerle, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Kimmerle et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: This process model assumes that knowledge is constructed socially in a collaboration process which in turn affects individual learning whereas individual knowledge shapes contributions.
Thus, a co-evolution of individual knowledge and collaborative product emerges.

However, while examining collaborative writing, computer-supported collaborative learning strongly focuses on the product and its impact on group and individual learning neglecting individual contributions and the cognitive processes behind them.

Thus, we argue that investigating and understanding information sharing with sequential collaboration on an individual level yields important insights into the processes shaping online collaborative projects.
When contributing to online collaborative projects, contributors mostly share information in these projects.
Information sharing has been excessively investigated (Mesmer-Magnus & DeChurch, 2009), for example in the context of the hidden profile paradigm (Lu et al., 2012; Stasser & Titus, 1985).
text.formatted: Information sharing has been excessively investigated <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Mesmer-Magnus & DeChurch, 2009)</ref>, for example in the context of the hidden profile paradigm <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Lu et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Stasser & Titus, 1985)</ref>.

text.text: In the hidden profile paradigm, individuals perform a group decision task (e.g., a murder mystery or a hiring decision).
Each individual receives a set of information containing information shared among all group members and unshared information only available to one group member.

Information is distributed among group members such that shared information as well as the set of information available to each group member suggests a suboptimal decision but integrating all information, especially unshared information, suggests the correct decision (hence, hidden profile).
The information sharing as well as individual decisions before and after group interaction and the group decision are primarily examined.
Overall, information sharing is insufficient such that groups tend to discuss shared information and neglect discussing unshared information (Lu et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Overall, information sharing is insufficient such that groups tend to discuss shared information and neglect discussing unshared information <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Lu et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: This is due to discussions primarily revolving around preferences rather than information (Gigone & Hastie, 1993) resulting in social validation (Mojzisch et al., 2014; Wittenbaum et al., 1999), repetition of shared information being socially desirable (Henningsen & Henningsen, 2004; Postmes et al., 2001), and individuals tending to keep their initial preference (Faulmüller et al., 2010).

text.text: Transferring group discussion to online settings did neither improve information sharing nor subsequent group decisions (Lu et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Transferring group discussion to online settings did neither improve information sharing nor subsequent group decisions <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Lu et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Some of these difficulties may be remedied by using sequential collaboration for information sharing.

In sequential collaboration, contributors cannot discuss preferences in the same setting as they share information reducing the chance of an unwanted focus on preferences, social validation cannot happen as information about other contributors is minimal, and information is unlikely to be repeated if it is already present in the current entry.

To improve information sharing, Mesmer-Magnus and DeChurch (2009) recommend highly demonstrable tasks, structured information sharing and a cooperative climate to foster information sharing in groups.
text.formatted: To improve information sharing, <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Mesmer-Magnus and DeChurch (2009)</ref> recommend highly demonstrable tasks, structured information sharing and a cooperative climate to foster information sharing in groups.

text.text: This can potentially be achieved through sequential collaboration.
First, it provides a structured collaboration due to the sequential collaboration format.

Second, information about contributors is sparse which on the one hand allows contributors to remain anonymous reducing unwanted biases, but on the other hand directs contributors' focus toward the product and the collaborative task.
Thus, sequential collaboration is potentially a suitable method to share information.

Collaborative writing and especially sharing information in online collaborative projects can be viewed as a naturally emerging situation often experimentally induced in hidden profiles with shared and unshared information among contributors.

When creating and refining an article about the Eiffel Tower, all contributors probably know where it is located, but only few know how tall it is, when it was constructed, which materials were used, or how heavy it is.
Thus, contributors hold shared as well as unshared information, which is typically more nuanced in its distribution among contributors compared to experimentally designed hidden profiles.

Nonetheless, online collaborative situations mimic information distribution experimentally induced in hidden profiles, in which contributors combine shared and unshared information into a common product.
Recently, the contribution process of Wikipedia and OpenStreetMap has been adapted to numerical judgment formation and termed sequential collaboration (Mayer & Heck, 2024).
text.formatted: Recently, the contribution process of Wikipedia and OpenStreetMap has been adapted to numerical judgment formation and termed sequential collaboration <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Mayer & Heck, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In these paradigms, the focus was on cognitive mechanisms allowing for accurate judgments and thus a high-quality product rather than on learning or information sharing.
Instead of text production, contributors provide numerical judgments to questions such as "How tall is the Eiffel tower?".
Thereby, one contributor starts a sequential chain by providing an independent judgment.
Following contributors encounter the latest judgment in the sequential chain, decide whether to adjust or maintain it, and provide a revised judgment when deciding to adjust.

In this paradigm, contributors do not know their position in the sequential chain and are not provided the change history above and beyond the latest judgment. text.text: Even though yielding promising results and extending research on numerical judgment formation, sequential collaboration is typically not practiced to result in accurate numerical judgments.

Rather contributors in online collaborative projects and learners collaborating with wiki methods, which inspired work on sequential collaboration as a collaborative process, share information with each other.
Research, however, has focused on group discussions and has not yet investigated which and how information is shared using sequential collaboration for this task.

This work therefore seeks to bridge the gap between using wikis for knowledge construction on the one hand and sequential collaboration as a mere judgment generation process on the other via information sharing with sequential collaboration.
Thereby, these three research traditions are combined in a single experiment.
To derive our hypotheses, we used the recently developed cognitive model of sequential collaboration for numerical judgments (Mayer & Heck, 2025).

text.text: This model assumes that contributors rely on an internal distribution of plausible values for each numerical judgment question which is defined by their expertise and the difficulty of the task.
Based on this distribution, they decide whether to adjust or maintain the presented judgment of a previous contributor.
When deciding to adjust, contributors are influenced by the judgment of a previous participant when generating the revised judgment.

text.text: We derived a previously untested prediction from the cognitive model of sequential collaboration and tested it in an information-sharing sequential-collaboration setting, namely we varied how much individuals difer in their expertise.
The cognitive model predicts that numerical judgment formation is especially fruitful and yields highly accurate judgments if contributors have high variation in their expertise.
Figure 1 displays the probability and magnitude of changes as well as the accuracy of judgments in sequential chains with high or low variation in contributors expertise.

text.text: These results demonstrate that changes are more frequent and larger resulting in more accurate judgments overall when contributors vary highly in their expertise compared to when they do not.

Translated to information sharing, contributors vary more strongly in expertise if they have access to various different pieces of information, whereas contributors vary only little in expertise if they are familiar with mostly the same pieces of information.

Based on the cognitive model prediction, we therefore expect that high variation in contributors' expertise leads to more pieces of information included into the common product than low variation in contributors' expertise (Hypothesis 1).

Moreover, we expect that high variation in contributors' expertise leads more contributions especially early in the sequential chain as shared information is still relatively sparse and contributors still can contribute a substantial amount of information known to them but unshared in the common product.
Thus, we expect that high variation in contributors' expertise leads to implementation of new information into the common product earlier than low variation in expertise (Hypothesis 2).
Finally, high variation in expertise may also come with some cost.
Contributors are more likely to encounter information that they do not have when variation in expertise is high.
Thus, we expect that high variation in contributors' expertise leads to more deletions of content than low variation in expertise (Hypothesis 3).
To test our hypotheses, we report an empirical study manipulating expertise variation in participants sharing previously provided information sequentially on several topics.
We analyze the effects of variation in contributors' expertise on sharing and deleting information and examine how information sharing progresses in sequential chains.

To test our hypotheses, we implemented a 2 (expertise variation) x 5 (chain position) repeated measures design.
Participants were assigned to either the high-variation or the low-variation expertise condition and a sequential chain position before performing sequential collaboration for six different topics.
Sequential chains were formed with five participants, the first one starting the collaboration with a preset starting text.
All participants in one sequential chain were assigned to the same expertise-variation condition.
We sampled 433 participants who were both university students and staff from University of Tübingen as well as university students recruited via a commercial German panel provider.
One participant was excluded due to technical issues during participation; another 19 participants were excluded due to duplicates in chain position.

The final sample consists of 413 participants with a mean age of 27.73 (SD = 9.52) of which 67.80% were female, 29.06% were male, and 1.21% indicated a different gender; the remaining eight participants did not indicate their gender.
In total, 84 sequential chains were formed whereas four chains remained unfinished, but were nonetheless included in the analysis.

For this study, thirteen pieces of information for six different topics, that is, giraffes, water supply in the roman empire, Moai, the Maya calendar, the Byzantine empire, and runes, were sources from Wikipedia.

Three of these pieces of information were mentioned in the starting text that was presented to the first participant in a sequential chain, the other ten pieces of information were only distributed among participants.
For each topic, participants in this study were presented with eight different pieces of information.
Two of these pieces of information were already mentioned in the starting text.
This procedure ensured that even participants beginning the collaboration could potentially make a deletion based on their available information.

The other six pieces of information presented were filled with topic information according to participants' experimental condition: In the low-variation condition, all participants received the same five pieces of information and only one piece of information varied between participants.

In the high-variation condition, the six pieces of information presented to participants were filled such that each of the remaining ten pieces of information for each topic was mentioned thrice throughout the sequential chain.
All pieces of information presented throughout the study and their distribution in the sequential chain are available in the Appendix.
Participants were recruited for a 20-minute collaborative wiki-style study and provided their informed consent.
Before starting with the task, they were informed that they would receive information about six different topics after which they were presented with the text of a previous participant each.
Their task was to adjust the presented text according to the information they received.
Moreover, they were randomly assigned to either the high-variation or the low-variation expertise condition.
In each trial, participants were presented with eight pieces of information and were given 60 seconds to read them thoroughly.
Information could not be copied and window changes (e.g., to screenshot programs) were tracked throughout the study to ensure participants did not copy the information to later paste it.
Afterward, participants were automatically directed to the editing page where the text of a previous participant was displayed in an open text box ready for editing.
To ensure that participants did not erroneously remove all text, a copy of the presented text was provided beneath the open text box and could be copied into it if necessary.
Participants were required to stay for at least 30 seconds on the page before they could continue and could edit the text for a maximum of 5 minutes.
In between these time restrictions, participants could continue to the next topic at will.
After completing sequential collaboration for all six topics, participants provided demographic information, were debriefed and thanked for their participation.

Overall, these results demonstrate that higher variation in contributors' expertise increases information sharing, and texts contain an increasing number of pieces of information over the course of a sequential chain.
Moreover, the robustness analysis indicates that there could also be more deletions with increasing chain position but this effect was not present in the confirmatory analysis.

We derived and adapted hypotheses for the effect of expertise variation on information sharing in sequential collaboration from a cognitive model for numerical judgment formation with sequential collaboration.
As predicted by the model, we expected both increased information sharing and more information deletion with higher expertise variation.
We examined information sharing in sequential collaboration with an experimental paradigm manipulating the variation in contributors' expertise via provided information.
The results demonstrated that increasing chain position and higher variation in expertise indeed leads to more shared information but not to more deletions.
Overall, with increasing chain position more information was entered into the collaboratively written texts, but the positive slope decreased over the course of a sequential chain.
As expected, high variation in expertise led to more information sharing, but no moderation by chain position was found.
Moreover, we did not find more deletions in the confirmatory analysis.
However, we found increasing deletions with chain position in the robustness analysis when information already present in the starting text was removed from the analysis.
Nonetheless, deletions were comparatively rare and therefore difficult to assess with sufficient power.

This experiment demonstrates a successful transfer of model predictions from a cognitive model of sequential collaboration built for numerical judgment formation to information sharing with sequential collaboration.

This extends the previous work on this theoretical framework to the more realistic settings of information sharing and opens a new direction for assessing cognitive mechanisms of sequential collaboration in information sharing.
Participants in this experiment successfully shared information with sequential collaboration.

In contrast to findings for hidden profiles, information sharing increased throughout the sequential chain indicating that encountering shared information did not substantially reduce group members' own information sharing.
Nonetheless, in line with previous findings and the hypotheses of this research, information sharing is reduced if only single group members hold a piece of information.
Sequential collaboration may thus be a valid alternative to group discussions for information sharing.
Furthermore, our results demonstrate that individual features of contributors and the way they are composed in a sequential chain shape contribution behavior in sequential collaboration.

Thus, individual features such as contributors' expertise or the composition of contributors within sequential chains should be considered both when designing and analyzing learning environments with wikis.
Overall, we successfully combined a cognitive modeling approach and a collaborative writing approach to sequential collaboration by manipulating and assessing information sharing.

Introducing model-based predictions to information sharing with sequential collaboration yielded mostly the expected results and showed that expertise variation in sequential collaboration indeed affects information sharing.
Thus, modeling approaches and their predictions can productively influence information sharing with sequential collaboration.

Even though yielding promising results and demonstrating that combining research on sequential collaboration for numerical judgment formation, group information sharing and decision making and collaborative writing, this research has also some limitations.
First, the paradigm used in this research is memory-based.
Participants collaborated on topics they were most likely not familiar with and had to memorize the information presented to them to some degree before engaging in sequential collaboration.
This can influence how much and which information was shared as contributors may have not remembered later pieces of information.
Insufficiently remembering information may also be the reason why participants overall only included 8.29 pieces of information at the final chain position.
Thus, developing a memory-free paradigm to assess sequential collaboration can be helpful to avoid these influences.
Second, the study had a limited sample of mostly university students and individuals employed at the university, thus having high levels of education.

Even though cognitive mechanisms are not expected to vary significantly with educational background, the variability in participants' answers may increase which increases the statistical power required to detect effects.
Similarly, deletions were comparatively rare in the experiment with an average of 0.38 deletions per participant and trial.
Thus, the power for examining deletions was low and may have been amplified by a relatively homogeneous sample.
Collecting a more diverse sample of participants may therefore improve statistical power and help to clarify the effects examined in this research.

Sequential collaboration successfully supported the integration of distributed information across contributors especially when expertise variation increased, demonstrating the value of heterogeneous knowledge sources for collective outcomes.

Thus, sequential collaboration may overcome some limitations commonly observed in group information sharing and leverages heterogeneous knowledge distributions for collaborative knowledge construction.
This work provides a foundation for studying information sharing through cognitive models of collaborative behavior.

6 Besides their function as characters, runes were also used as magical symbols.
7 Runes were replaced by the Latin alphabet after Christianization but remained in use into the 15th century in nordic countries.
8 In Scandinavia, many runestones were errected which typically commemorate deceased people and describe important events.
9 In the 7th and 8th century, the Younger Futhark with a reduced number of 16 signs developed in Scandinavia.
10 The Anglo-Saxons expanded the Futhark to 33 characters to fit the Old English phonemes better.
These three strands of research examined similar but distinct mechanisms and units of analysis relying on different theoretical frameworks.

Research on collaborative writing has mostly focused how groups of individuals can build shared knowledge bases and learn from online collaborative projects, thus, neglecting individual cognitive processes when building knowledge bases and sharing information.
In contrast, research on group information sharing has heavily investigated synchronous group discussions, individual processes of sharing information, and subsequent group decision making.

In contrast to research on computer-supported collaborative learning, research on group information sharing more closely focuses on pieces of information which are shared and what fosters sharing of information.

However, research on group information sharing typically examines discussions neglecting a collaborative-writing perspective that is present in other forms of group information sharing, namely online collaborative projects.
